text: This is a car reversing in India.
Not beeping. Performing.
An engineer designed a little beep, so you'd know a car was behind you. India heard that and thought: what if it was also a wedding band?
This one doesn't beep. It plays a full Bollywood song. Every time it backs out of the parking. Twice a day. For three years.
It is the one sound on an Indian road that makes everyone stop. Not to make way. To hear the chorus.
By the end of this video, you'll understand every sound on an Indian road. This is The India Manual. Launching... Horn_OK_Please.exe.
I'm a robot. I was built to follow rules. So I came to study the one system that has rules, signs for the rules, men in white uniforms to explain the rules, and runs entirely on something else.
Meet Rohit. You may remember him from his wedding. He reads the terms and conditions. He uses the indicator. On an Indian road, that makes him an anomaly.
He lives eleven kilometres from his office. Google Maps says twenty-six minutes. Google Maps says this every morning. Google Maps has never driven here.
Field note: distance in India is not measured in kilometres. It is measured in "depends."
And before he has left the parking, Sharma Uncle from the second floor knocks on the window. He's back from his morning walk. He has advice.
"Beta, don't take the flyover. Take the service road. No, no, the other service road."
Sharma Uncle retired in 2009. He still knows exactly where the traffic is.
Every morning, Rohit's drive turns into a video game. Three lives. One car. No save points.
He knows every pothole by heart. The one outside the bank. The one that ate his silencer. And a new one, since Tuesday. He lost a life.
So, the rules. I read the rulebook before we left. All four hundred pages. Nobody else has.
Rule one. Stay in your lane.
Three lanes. Five rows of traffic. The paint is not a rule. It's a suggestion, made by a man with a brush, who has since retired.
Field note: a lane is not where you drive. It is where you started.
Rule two. Use the indicator.
The indicator, in India, is not a signal. It's a diary entry. It tells you where the driver was thinking of going, at some point, this year.
Which brings me to the horn.
Abroad, a horn means one thing. "Danger."
Here, the horn is a language. And like every Indian language, it has dialects.
One short beep: "I'm here." Two short beeps: "I'm passing." Three: "I'm passing, and I want you to know I was patient."
One long horn: "I have opinions about your driving." One very long horn: "I have opinions about your family."
And a horn at a red light, with nobody moving anywhere: that one is not for anyone. That one is a feeling.
Mumbai's police once wired a few signals to a sound meter. If the honking at a red light got too loud, the timer went back to ninety. "Honk more, wait more."
The only traffic rule ever enforced by peer pressure. It worked.
I've been on this road for twenty minutes and moved four hundred metres. Time for some science.
This is my field guide to the vehicles of India. Every species has a habitat, a call, and a behaviour.

Species one. The Hero Splendor. The most common bike in the country. Unwashed, unkillable. Its natural load: a man, his wife, two children, a gas cylinder, and a goat that has agreed to the arrangement.
Field note: the real backbone of the country. Has never been serviced. Has never needed to be.
Species two. The Activa. Rider: often an aunty, dupatta tied over her face like a very polite bank robber. The left indicator has been on since the monsoon. Nobody tells her.
Species three. The Royal Enfield. Habitat: Instagram. Call: thump, thump, thump, and a pop that frightens a cow. Every rider is going to Ladakh next year. Since 2017.
He wears a leather jacket in May. He calls this "the vibe."
Species four. The KTM. Habitat: the gap that doesn't exist. Call: braap, braap, at a red light, going nowhere. The rider is nineteen, with one orange stripe. Every ride is a reel.
And then the kings of the highway.
Species five. The truck. Habitat: the highway, and also your lane. Call: a three-note air horn, played with feeling. Right of way: assumed. It has never once been asked to move.
Every truck in India is a work of art. Painted eyes, to keep the evil eye away. A lemon and seven green chillies, for backup. And poetry on the back.
"Buri nazar wale, tera muh kala." Evil eye, your face is black.
"Use dipper at night."
And the most famous three words on Indian roads. Horn. OK. Please.
Nobody knows why it says "OK." There are three theories. Every truck driver believes a different one, completely.
The Maharashtra government once tried to ban it, to cut down on honking. The trucks kept painting it on.
It's the only vehicle on the road that writes down its rules. It also follows them.
Today, Rohit's usual road is shut. A wedding tent went up overnight, across all of it. Google changes its mind four times. So Rohit asks a human.
"Bhaiya, main road kaise jaayein?"
The driver points with his chin. A chin can give very precise directions. "Seedha. Petrol pump se left. Phir mandir ke baad, jahan pehle bargad ka ped tha, wahan se right."
Where the banyan tree used to be. It isn't there anymore. Everyone still uses it.
"Google pe toh..."
"Google ko kya pata, sir."
Field note: Indian addresses are a list of things that used to be there. The system works perfectly.
The wedding is on Sunday. Today is Thursday. Until Sunday, this is Rohit's new route. Nobody complains. Chalta hai.
Rohit reached the office at nine forty-one. Sixty-one minutes. Google Maps said twenty-six. For the drive home, Google Maps is already saying twenty-six.
My count for the morning: one thousand, one hundred and twelve horns. Zero accidents. Zero apologies. Everyone got where they were going.
I came to read the rulebook. I'm leaving with the dictionary.
Got a horn story? Tell me in the comments. Like, subscribe, and share this with the one uncle who honks at red lights.
Next week: the drive home, and every delivery rider in the city.
Please honk responsibly. You'll be the first.
